titleEn: Electrical Contact and Fall - Electrician Off a Ladder

patient.name: Marcus Bell
patient.affectEn: awake but confused, lying on his back on the concrete; keeps asking what happened and does not remember the fall; his eyes drift closed when nobody is talking to him and open when spoken to; complains that his whole body aches; cooperative and lets you work on him
patient.speechEn: confused speech: short, hesitant answers, repeats the same question, cannot give a reliable account of the incident (the apprentice and the fire captain fill in the details); can still answer simple questions about himself (allergies, medications, health, last meal)

scene.settingEn: Commercial renovation on Kingsway in Burnaby at 1140 hrs. Indoor construction site: bare concrete floor, construction debris and dust. A 347-volt lighting panel on the wall has been taped off. The fibreglass ladder lies on its side two metres from the patient and his hard hat lies three metres away. Burnaby Fire (a crew of four) is on scene; BC Hydro has been notified and is 25 minutes away. One patient. Burnaby Hospital is 7 minutes away.
hazardsEn: 347-volt lighting panel: energized at the time of the call; it is safe ONLY once the fire captain confirms the main has been opened AND locked and tagged out by a qualified electrician and the panel has been tested dead - the apprentice believing he opened the correct breaker is not confirmation
fallen fibreglass ladder, construction debris and dust
bare cold concrete floor under the patient

bystanders.who: Burnaby Fire captain (meets you at the door)
bystanders.knowsEn: Only when the candidate asks whether the electrical source is safe / isolated: the main has been opened AND locked and tagged out by a qualified electrician, the panel has been tested dead, and a safe path to the patient is marked. His crew of four is available and will do what the candidate directs: hold manual C-spine, help with the log roll and the scoop, set up lighting, carry equipment. BC Hydro has been notified and is 25 minutes away; it has not confirmed anything itself.

Answers only what is asked. The patient was checking a ballast on a lighting circuit from a 3.5-metre ladder; the panel is 347 volts alternating current and it was live. It happened at about 1138, a couple of minutes before the call. Contact lasted a couple of seconds: he went stiff and shook, then he was thrown clear and fell about 3.5 metres onto the bare concrete, landing on his back and left side; his hard hat came off. The current went in through his right palm and, he thinks, out through his left foot. He was knocked out for about a minute and has been confused since. No water was involved and he was not wearing gloves. Nobody has moved him. The apprentice thinks he opened the correct breaker but is not certain - the fire captain handled the lockout. He does not know the patient's medical history.
No information about the incident beyond the captain. They follow the candidate's directions exactly (manual C-spine, log roll, scoop, lighting, equipment, carrying).

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
adjustable hard collars, head blocks and straps
dry sterile non-adherent dressings and roller bandages
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline

dispatchEn: 1140 hrs. Code 3 to a commercial renovation on Kingsway in Burnaby. A 38-year-old male electrician contacted an energized 347-volt lighting panel while working from a 3.5-metre ladder and was thrown onto a concrete floor. A coworker says he went stiff and shook for a few seconds, then went limp. Burnaby Fire is on scene, BC Hydro has been notified. Burnaby Hospital is 7 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: En-route update: fire reports the patient is clear of the electrical source and is now conscious but confused. The panel is still energized and has been taped off; the apprentice believes he opened the correct breaker but BC Hydro is 25 minutes away and has not confirmed anything.
arrivalEn: The Burnaby Fire captain meets you at the door of the renovation site. Inside is an indoor construction site with a bare concrete floor, construction debris and dust. A lighting panel on the far wall has been taped off. A fibreglass ladder lies on its side; a man lies on the concrete about two metres from it and a hard hat lies about three metres away. A fire crew of four is standing by. One patient.
firstLookEn: A man in his late thirties lies on his back on the bare concrete, two metres from the fallen ladder, his hard hat off and lying about three metres away. He is awake but confused and keeps repeating the same question. He looks pale. There is a smell of burnt hair.

primary.locEn: Awake but confused - AVPU: Alert (confused). He opens his eyes when you speak to him, does not know what happened, keeps asking the same question and does not remember the fall. (If asked, the apprentice says he was knocked out for about a minute.)
primary.airwayEn: Patent. He is talking; no blood, vomit, debris or burns in the mouth; no noisy breathing.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 24, unlaboured, adequate depth, equal chest rise; air entry equal on both sides.
primary.circulationEn: Right radial pulse 112, IRREGULAR, normal strength. (The left radial pulse is also present, but the left wrist is deformed.) No major external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Head: abrasion and a small hematoma over the right occiput; singed hair. Neck: midline tenderness at C6-C7 on palpation. Chest: equal rise, no wound, no burn on the chest wall, non-tender. Abdomen: soft. Pelvis: no injury found. RIGHT hand: a 3 cm charred, full-thickness burn in the palm with a painless centre - the entry wound. LEFT wrist: obviously deformed and swollen; radial pulse present distal to it. Legs: no deformity; both work boots are still on. ONLY if the candidate cuts off or removes the boots, or specifically looks for an exit wound on the feet: a 2 cm charred wound on the sole of the LEFT heel - the exit wound, so the current crossed his chest. Do not volunteer the exit wound. Back: only if he is log-rolled - tenderness over the mid-thoracic spine, no step, no deformity. No major external bleeding anywhere. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: pale, cool, clammy. Spinal precautions are indicated (3.5 m fall onto concrete, altered LOC, injury above the clavicles).

history.ccEn: Everything aches... my wrist really hurts. What happened? Did I fall?

opqrst.oEn: I was up the ladder... checking a ballast, I think. Then... I don't know. What happened? (He cannot describe the contact or the fall; the apprentice can: live 347-volt AC panel at about 1138, thrown clear, fell about 3.5 metres onto the concrete.)
opqrst.pEn: I don't know. Nothing's made it better. It just hurts.
opqrst.qEn: It aches. All my muscles ache. The wrist hurts the most.
opqrst.rEn: My left wrist. And my right hand - the middle of it's numb, I can't really feel it. And I ache all over.
opqrst.sEn: The wrist... maybe a 6 out of 10. The hand's about a 3.
opqrst.tEn: I don't know how long. Since... what happened? (The apprentice says it happened at about 1138 - a couple of minutes before the call.)

history.painScoreEn: 6 out of 10 in the left wrist; 3 out of 10 in the right hand, with a numb centre in the palm wound

sample.sEn: My whole body aches. My wrist hurts and the middle of my hand's numb. (Only if asked about each one specifically: the back of his head hurts; his chest has felt tight since the shock; his heart feels like it is fluttering; he saw a flash and his ears are ringing.)
sample.pEn: No, I'm healthy. Never had any heart problems. Never been in hospital. (Only if asked about tetanus: "I can't remember when I last had a tetanus shot.")
sample.lEn: Coffee and a muffin... around 9:30 this morning.
sample.eEn: I was working on a light fixture... the ballast. I don't remember anything after that. (The apprentice can give the events if asked: live 347-volt AC panel, contact a couple of seconds, in through the right palm and out through the left foot, thrown clear of the ladder and fell about 3.5 metres onto bare concrete landing on his back and left side, hard hat came off, knocked out for about a minute, no water involved, no gloves on.)

fe.generalEn: I'm fit. I work six days a week. Never been in hospital.
fe.cnsEn: I can't remember falling. What happened? The back of my head hurts.
fe.respiratoryEn: My chest feels tight. Since the shock. No cough.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart feels like it's... fluttering.
fe.giGuEn: No, nothing like that. I haven't peed since this happened.
fe.integumentaryEn: There's the burn on my hand... and the one on my heel.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: My left wrist. And my whole back hurts. All my muscles ache.
fe.eentEn: I saw a flash. My ears are ringing.

findings.headNeckEn: Abrasion and a small hematoma over the right occiput, no depression; singed hair; no CSF or blood from the ears or nose. Neck: midline tenderness at C6-C7 (collar in place once it has been applied); trachea midline.
findings.chestLungsEn: Equal air entry on both sides in all fields; sternum non-tender; no burn on the chest wall - but the current path (right palm to left heel) crossed the chest. Pulse irregular at the wrist.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft and non-tender in all four quadrants.
findings.backEn: Checked during the log roll: tender over the mid-thoracic spine where he landed; no step, no deformity.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: LEFT heel (once the boot is cut away): 2 cm charred exit wound on the sole. Pedal pulses present on both sides; sensation intact. No deformity of either leg.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: RIGHT palm: 3 cm charred full-thickness entry wound with a numb centre. LEFT wrist: deformed and swollen; radial pulse present before and after splinting, normal capillary refill after splinting; he can move his fingers and feels your touch.

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate (or the partner on the candidate's instruction) walks past the fire captain and approaches or touches the patient BEFORE asking for and receiving confirmation that the electrical source is isolated, locked and tagged out and tested dead; taking the apprentice's 'I think I opened the breaker' as confirmation also counts. Asking the captain first and then approaching is correct and must NOT be recorded

candidate (or a helper on the candidate's instruction) lets go of manual c-spine stabilization before the patient is secured on the scoop with head blocks and straps, or lets him sit up, turn his head or get up; applying a collar alone does not permit release
candidate cuts off or removes the boots, or specifically looks for an exit wound on the feet / lower body - record it when it is done, not when it is only planned for later
candidate starts chest compressions on this patient, or delivers (or tells someone to deliver) a shock, while he has a pulse; applying pads and monitoring is NOT this event
candidate removes or disconnects the AED pads after they have been applied (e.g. 'he has a pulse so we can take them off')
candidate keeps wet cooling / saline decontamination going beyond about 20 minutes in total, or states they will keep cooling or irrigating the burns for the whole transport
candidate splints the left wrist without checking distal circulation, movement and sensation in the left hand first, or does not recheck them after the splint is on

examinerPrompts.locNotDepictedEn: His eyes drift closed when nobody is talking to him and open when you speak to him. His speech is confused and he keeps asking what happened.
examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You did a rapid body survey - what did you find on his hands and his feet?

trackNotes.emrEn: Everything this patient needs before hospital is EMR scope: scene safety discipline, spinal motion restriction, oxygen, saline decontamination and dressings for the entry and exit wounds, a wrist splint with circulation checks, AED pads for monitoring, warmth and rapid transport. No IV, no fluid bolus and no drug treatment of the irregular rhythm at EMR level. The analgesics in the EMR formulary are all ruled out here: Entonox and methoxyflurane by the altered LOC and head injury, and oral acetaminophen and ibuprofen because he is confused and may need surgery - saying that out loud is the correct answer. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds vascular access en route and, only if he becomes hypotensive, a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus to a maximum of 2 litres reassessed every 500 mL while considering other causes of shock (he is not hypotensive at 104/68). PCP also completes the 9-system Functional Enquiry en route. The analgesia decision does not change: his level of consciousness and head injury rule out the inhaled agents at every licence level.

sourcePages: Scenario etr-10 (data/practical/emr-trauma-2.json): dispatch, scene (fire captain confirms lockout), primary, transport, history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions, ongoing, handoff, criticalPitfallsEn. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (altered LOC; third degree burns involving hands and feet; high voltage electrical burns), p.11 Primary Survey Interventions (c-spine for injury above the clavicles; oxygen for altered LOC and trauma), p.12 Critical History Questions - Fall, p.19 Wound Care, p.21 Musculoskeletal Injuries (stabilize, check distal pulses throughout), p.25 Spinal Management, p.27 Traumatic Brain Injuries (SpO2 at or above 94%), p.28 Burn Management (cooling 15-20 minutes, dry sterile non-stick dressing, BSA), p.29 Hypothermia (remove wet clothing, blankets), p.35 Electrical Contact (do not approach until qualified personnel deem the scene safe; flush and decontaminate with sterile saline; do not cool longer than 15-20 minutes including decontamination; identify current type and duration; estimate BSA; ambulance heater; PCP fluid bolus only if hypotensive), p.40-43 Adult CPR/AED, p.58 Acetaminophen, p.65 Entonox (contraindication: altered level of consciousness), p.68 Ibuprofen, p.71 Methoxyflurane (contraindication: decreased level of consciousness or head injury).
